title: The Taped Knuckle
passages:
"No," Kass said, into the set, and loud enough that the open channel carried it up the ore line to Anza's board and out onto the morning desk's relief overflow, where it would sit in a log until somebody with a clean record read it. "Nobody signs anything. Not on my channel."

"Dispatcher," Marlowe said. His voice came through the pump bulb — the old brass horn bolted above the door, spliced into the set at some point before either of them was born — thin but clear, with a splinted man's careful breathing behind it. "You clear loads. You don't clear me."

"It's a trade, not a load."

"It's my body, and I outrank you on it. Desk can requisition cargo. Nobody requisitions a man's ribs but the man." A pause, a wet cough, then: "Kass. Sign it. I've had worse Tuesdays."

Under his voice, faint, a squeak of rubber on a hand pump, in and out, patient as a metronome. Then Rhea, close to the bulb, none of the patience in her voice at all.

"Kass. Take the deal."

"Rhea—"

"Four restarts left. Four. After that I'm squeezing the bag with my hands for however long it takes you to walk back up that grade, and my arm is already gone from the shoulder down." Inhale, squeak, exhale. "I don't want Voss. I want what's on that puck. A reseal carries a time. Get me the time off the sender, get me the six cases, put the scrubbers on a rig. That's all I'm asking."

"The time tells us who shut it," Kass said. "Not whether Voss tells the truth about the rest."

"Nobody's feeding anything," Voss said, from the bench. He had the flat, unbothered look of a man who'd erased himself so thoroughly that weather had more claim on him than people did. "You've got twenty minutes of daylight and a reclaimer with a clearance that turns before eight. Sign, and the scrubbers are yours by seven."

Kass looked at the stack. Eleven cases, Anza's marks on every one, corded and pucked, sitting on a dead pump station's floor like they'd been raised there.

"I want to look at one."

"Nothing in here is free," Brill said. She had her lamp in one hand, a kerosene thing with a cracked chimney, and she held it the way other people hold a wrench. "Not even the light."

"Ospina," Kass said. "What does your ring buy in this room?"

Ospina had been standing with their coat still on, the dirty mark on their authority sitting there like a stain nobody could see but everybody could price. They put their hand out flat. "A receiving counter. Her stock reads Bay 4 sent and Culvert Nine received, in her own ledger, in her own hall. It stops being stolen."

Brill's chin came up. "It also puts my station's name in a ledger."

"Your winter's already got a name on it," Kass said. "Eleven seals off Anza's down-line. Only question left is whether the name is thief or receiver, and that gets decided at eight either way."

Brill set the lamp on the bench and stepped back, which in that room was a signature.

Ospina lifted the nearest case enough to turn it. The sender puck was a steel disk the size of a thumbnail, crimped over the seal wire on the lid: the only thing on a rig that says who shut it and when. Its face is a shallow strike, meant to be read flat under a powered reader, and the pump station had no power, so there was nothing to do but tilt it into the flame and let the light rake across the metal.

"Talk while they look," Marlowe said, over the bulb.

"Quiet," Kass said. "Ospina. Whose?"

Ospina turned the puck a quarter inch. The strike came up out of the steel in pieces, bright where the metal was cut and dark where it was pressed, and Ospina looked at it for a long enough time that the pump bulb hissed and Rhea's hand went around again at the far end.

Behind them, Miko put one hand flat on the overlap log and kept it there.

"Kass," Ospina said. "Hold the trade."

Ospina did not tilt the puck into the flame. They turned the case and held the lid where the lamp's light ran flat along the crimp — the metal ferrule squeezed over the seal wire where the lid's two ears meet, the one part of a case you can't get past without cutting.

"Talk," Kass said.

"Bay 4 Shift 2 on the strike. All eleven, I'd put my ring on it." Ospina's thumbnail went along the crimp and stopped. "Crimp's chipped. There's a notch out of the shoulder, about so." They held up a fingertip. "A die stamps the strike and squeezes the wire in the same pull, so whatever's wrong with the face is wrong with the shoulder too. This die's got a piece out of it."

"File it," Kass said.

"Then the notch moves and the old ones stay put. You can't file a die and un-file it." Ospina set the case down. "I've pulled Bay 4 crimps for nine years. Voss's is square. Square shoulder, every time, like a stamp on a ration card."

"That's mine," Voss said. "Never filed a day in my life." He didn't get up. He took a brass die out of his coat and set it on the bench without looking at it, a man putting down a cup. The face was a square with a flat bar across it, the edges still sharp.

Ospina reached into their own coat and set a second die beside it. Steel, the strike face cut as a crescent with a bar across the belly, and a bite out of the lower horn the size of a thumbnail.

Nobody said anything. The pump bulb hissed.

Ospina picked up the crescent and laid the bitten horn against the notch in the crimp. It seated like a key.

"All eleven," Ospina said.

"Say the rest," Kass said.

"It's been in my coat since Kettering. I found it in the tool void on a northbound med rig the night of the twenty-first." They didn't look at Miko. "Bay 4's. I'm Bay 4 seal authority. I know what comes out of that shop." Ospina sat the crescent on the bench between the two brass-and-steel. "Two dies sealed Anza's eleven. One of them's been riding around in an Anza coat for two days."

"Not mine," Voss said.

"Nobody said it was yours," Kass said. "We said it was in the room."

Voss got up off the bench. It was the first time he'd stood since they came in, and he came as far as the lamp and stopped, looking at the crescent the way a man looks at his own name on a board he thought he'd wiped.

"Where did you get that."

"You heard the lady's coat," Ospina said. "Tool void. Bay 4."

"There's one crescent die on the Interior," Voss said. "It's been in a drawer at the Kettering morning desk since before I could stamp. Whoever had it in that void walked past me twice that night and I never turned around." His voice had lost the flatness. It had edges now. "Who else was in there with it."

The pump bulb hissed. At Anza, rubber squeaked on a hand pump, in and out.

"Later," Ospina said.

"Now."

"You want it on Kass's open channel? Half the relief overflow's listening, and the rest gets it at eight."

Rhea's voice came through the bulb, close and flat. "Kass. The receiving mark. Whose is it, because it isn't any of ours, and I want to know who Anza's been feeding."

Kass reached across Ospina for the case.

Behind them, Miko took her hand off the overlap log, one finger at a time, and put it in her coat pocket.

Kass turned the case so the puck faced the horn and keyed the set off the tight line to Anza and onto the wide one — the whole ore line, the relief overflow, every desk that would be reading a log at eight and pretending it hadn't.

"You want to know who walked past you in that void," Kass said to Voss. "The man in the box saw him. Marlowe. Say it again, slow, for the room."

The pump bulb carried the breathing first, and under it Rhea's hand pump, still squeaking, still patient, still four. Then Marlowe.

"Two of them at the lid," he said. "One had the stamp — square shoulder, I felt it bite the wire over my chest. The other had tape wound up his right knuckles to the second joint, gray gone black at the edges. Clean voice. Like it didn't cost him anything." A breath. "He held the lid down and counted me under it, out loud, the way you count a load you're not scared of. *Twenty-nine. Thirty.* Then the light went out."

The bulb hissed. Nobody in the pump hall moved.

"You heard him," Kass said. "Tape on the right hand, clean voice. You're the stamp, Voss. So who's the count?"

For a breath Voss looked like he'd go back to being weather. Then he reached across the bench, past his square die and Ospina's crescent, and turned the puck up into the lamplight himself, the way a man shows a wound he's decided to own.

"Eleven cases off Anza's down-line," he said. "I resealed them at 05:52. Bay 4, Shift 2, my mark on every strike. At 21:47 I sealed the loader in as ballast — databus already cut, so the box would read warm the whole way north — and I signed the pod out myself. Ballast. That's mine. All of it's mine." The flatness had a seam in it now. "I'm not putting any of it on the other one."

"Kass." Teodoro, from Anza, fast and helpful, the way he was about things nobody had asked him. "Give it back to me. Times. Clean, for the board log."

"Teodoro—"

"The drawer's open. *Twenty-one forty-seven, sealed the loader in as ballast.* Go on. *Oh-five fifty-two, resealed eleven.* And the sign-out — what did you sign the pod out as?"

"Ballast," Voss said, to the puck.

"Ballast," Teodoro said, and read the whole of it back into the set once, slow, every word going down into the drawer at Anza that keeps what it's told. Then he read it a second time — because the first time a man says a thing it can still be weather, and the second time it's a record, and a record is the one thing on the Interior you can't rub out with a chipped crescent or a clean morning.

Kass watched Voss hear it go.

He had wiped himself off the Kettering board so clean that morning the desk had nothing left to read — no strike, no flag, no name but the one he'd walked in here to sell. One clean morning. That was the whole of what the erasing had bought him.

And he'd just spent it out loud, on an open channel, to a room full of relief desks, to find out who held the lid.

"*Ah*," Voss said, very quietly, and sat back down.

"Not mine," Voss said. He had his hands back on his knees and the flat look back on his face, a man waiting out a shift change. "I stamp, I sign, I reseal. Counting is the other one's trade."

"Somebody counted," Kass said.

"Somebody did. He was standing at my elbow. Ask him for the voice, I'll give you the shoulder." A tip of the head toward the bulb. "You want the count on me you'll have to invent it, and you've already got the whole strike."

"The whole strike," Ospina agreed. "Twice, on an open channel."

"I did." Something moved across Voss's face that on another man would have been satisfaction. "Doesn't make me the count."

Ospina pulled the case back over the bench. "Then give her the rule. Out loud. There's a drawer open at Anza that keeps what it's told."

Voss hooked a thumb under the crimp like a man opening a letter he'd already read.

"A sender puck's half a seal," he said. "Mine strikes the mark and squeezes the wire, both in one pull. But the ferrule won't set unless there's a live receiving ring in the other jaw, closing at the same time. No ring, the wire springs back, the ferrule sits proud, and you've got a box with a dent in it. Down-line reads the ring side first. The ring's what makes it a seal instead of a lid."

"So you needed a ring," Kass said.

"I needed a ring nobody would come looking for. Not Bay 4. Shift 1 and Shift 2 count their rings at shift end, and a live counter under my eleven puts my name on them twice." He pushed the case away. "So I hired off the overflow."

"Explain overflow."

"The morning desk keeps a list of rings it lends out when a shift comes up short. Relief hands, day rate. You wear the desk's ring for a shift and you give it back. Badge 2244." A shrug. "Paid in freight. Nobody writes a name on freight."

"Freight," Brill said, from the wall. "Everybody on this line pays in freight and nobody signs. That's how a full storeroom gets a hole in it."

"Whose freight," Kass said.

"Not mine. I don't have freight. I have a stamp."

"Two two four four," Kass said, to the set. "Teodoro. Run it."

"Running." Then, because he could never wait to be asked: "A badge isn't a man, it's a credential — the desk issues the number to a ring, the ring goes to whoever picks up the shift, so the board can say what was sealed and never say by whom. That's the entire purpose of overflow." Paper moved somewhere at Anza. "Two two four four. Relief overflow seal ring, Kettering morning desk, live from twenty-one hundred on the twenty-first. One counter against it tonight. Twenty-one forty-seven. No seal number, no cargo line, one receiving ring."

"That's my lid," Marlowe said, through the bulb.

"No name on it," Teodoro said. "Overflow never takes one." His voice changed. "Kass. It's on a docket."

"Whose docket."

"The 08:00 review. Line four." A rustle. "Ospina's ring is line nine. Same review, same desk, same morning. Two two four four is flagged for closure at eight — ring pulled, badge retired, reissued to whoever comes up short on Shift 2 by the afternoon board. After eight there's no badge on any list. There's no overflow list."

The pump bulb hissed. At Anza the rubber went in and out, in and out.

"So at eight the desk erases the man who held your lid," Ospina said. "Clean. With a time on it and a signature under it."

"Not my problem," Voss said.

"It's everybody's problem in this hall," Kass said. "Rhea, you copy that?"

"Copy." Flat, close to the horn. "Fenn's clearance turns before eight and he's twenty minutes out. Whatever you're doing with a badge, do it before he's up that grade."

"Then we do it now." Kass keyed the set off the wide channel — the relief overflow could keep the eight o'clock version — and turned around. "Miko. You rode north in a tool void."

Miko had not said one word since Kettering. She reached out, moved the overlap log two inches nearer, and put her elbow on it.

"I've been in a lot of voids," she said.

"Think about which one had a desk drawer's die in it. At eight that number stops belonging to anybody, and you're the only one standing here who was in the room with it."

"Ask me something I can afford," Miko said.

Brill came off the wall, picked up her lamp where she'd left it, and set it down again in the middle of the bench — square, deliberate, between the brass die and the steel one — so all three strikes sat in one pool of light.

"Play the count," she said.

"It's in the drawer at Anza," Teodoro offered.

"Not the drawer. The man." Brill folded her arms. "I count a floor every night off the totalizer, and a totalizer doesn't care what a drawer thinks it heard. Play the count."

Kass keyed the set back to the tight line. "Marlowe. The lid again."

"Twenty-eight." The bulb carried it thin, with the breathing under it. "Twenty-nine. Thirty. Then the corner came down and the light went."

"Anything else he said?"

A breath, and under it the squeak of rubber. "He said, *put it down as anything you like, I'm paid in freight.*"

Brill didn't move.

Saul had come two steps in from the door with the tally clipboard held against their chest and the pencil behind their ear, and Brill looked at Saul's hands the way she looked at a scale she hadn't decided about yet. Clean knuckles. No tape.

"On the ninth," she said. "Four crates off this floor. Anza marks, down-line marks, corded and pucked, same as that stack." She tipped her chin at the eleven. "Man came up my grade with a clipboard and every line on it filled in. That's how I knew he was desk and not a thief. A thief leaves you blanks. A desk writes down what it's taking so the taking has a number, and a number is the only thing on this line that comes back for you."

"And he paid you," Kass said.

"He paid me in line paper." Flat. "Requisition stock. The desk's own paper — no signature needed on it, because the stock number traces to a drawer and the drawer traces to a man. Better than a signature. I can forge a signature."

"So where's the paper," Ospina said.

"Under the bench, in me." Brill reached down, came up with a dented canteen, shook it, set it back. "I couldn't keep it. My station's name on desk stock in this hall is the same as my station's name on a board at eight. So I tore it in strips and chewed it and swallowed it and drank half a canteen to get it down. Twenty minutes. Tasted ink till the next shift." She looked at the lamp. "Four crates went north on a rig I don't have a number for, and I've been short that much winter ever since, and I never saw his face, because he kept the board up between us the whole time."

"Kass." Rhea, close to the horn. "I'm at three. Be quick at whatever this is."

"Working," Kass said.

Brill put both hands flat on the bench, one on either side of the lamp.

"Ospina. Out loud, in this hall, with the horn open. The tape." She waited. "Was it on the hand that held my crate cord, or the hand that held the lid?"

Ospina didn't take long. "The lid. Gray to the second joint on the right, and Marlowe was under it with a light in his eyes. I'll swear that at eight."

"Right hand," Brill said.

"Right."

"Mine was the left." Her voice stayed level, which was worse than if it hadn't. "Taped to the second joint, gray gone black at the edges, holding my clipboard flat so I could read my own numbers off it while I signed nothing. Left hand. Same tape. Same knuckles. Same black."

Nobody said anything. The pump bulb hissed, and at Anza the rubber went in, out, in.

"So either two men came up my grade," Brill said, "or one man did and he can't keep his own hands straight."

Voss, from the bench, without lifting his head: "There were two of us in Bay 4."

"I know how many were in Bay 4." Brill picked up the lamp. "I'm asking how many walked up my grade." She turned to Kass, and the light swung off the stack and onto the corded lids. "That badge stops belonging to anybody at eight, and the name's still off it. You've got till Fenn's lights are on my grade to put a name to two two four four in this hall, out loud, where the horn can carry it." She turned the wick down until the room went the color of a shut hand. "Then we'll all find out what my rule is worth."

Brill turned the wick back up until the bench had edges again.

"My rule," she said, "is nothing for a man and nothing for a promise. Four years I've run this hall on it, through two dry winters and a shift that walked out on me in the dark. It's the only thing on the Interior that never once lied to me." She looked down the row of lids. "I'm breaking it once. I want the horn open while I do it, so if it goes wrong I'm not explaining myself twice."

"Terms," Kass said.

"The eleven walk against a chain that closes clean. Sender's strike, receiver's counter, one live ring in the cradle, and I read the strike out of the steel myself before anything goes on a cart. Scrubbers first — six cases by the grate before the other five move an inch." She put her palm flat on the bench. "And a name behind two two four four, said out loud in this hall, before Fenn's lights are on my grade. That's the voiding. Not a promise. A name."

"Badges don't carry names," Voss said.

"Then somebody in this room knows one anyway."

Voss stood. He crossed to the nearest case and stood over it with his hands loose, the way he'd stood over the puck, and this time he was looking past it at the pump bulb.

"Ballast doesn't get terms," he said. "Ballast gets a weight and a line. Loader. Give me your line. Cargo line, seal number, tare. Freight's got a number. Freight never argues at a lid."

The bulb carried the breathing first, and under it the rubber going in and out, in and out, three.

"Marlowe," Marlowe said. "One man. Bunk at Anza relay shop, listed crew, countersigned on a live ring by the Bay 4 seal authority, who is standing about four feet from you with a chip out of their die." A breath, and the wet catch behind it. "Contents: one man, one splint, one patched diaphragm, still here. Count was thirty. Write it down however you like, Voss. Don't write ballast. Ballast doesn't come back up a grade and ask who held the lid."

"He's one man," Rhea said, close to the horn, "and he's spoken for."

Ospina took off their right glove and set it on the bench.

"Say the rule again," they said. "Yours. Out loud, for the drawer."

"A sender crimp won't set without a live receiving ring closing in the other jaw," Voss said. "No ring, the wire springs back."

"And you couldn't use a Bay 4 ring, so you hired the overflow, and you just spent the last clean morning you ever bought saying so on an open channel." Ospina turned their hand over. The ring sat on the third finger, dull with shop grease, the flag on it invisible and worth more than everything stacked on the floor. "Mine's live till eight. Flagged, contested, doesn't matter, it closes. So here's your chain. I close the ring side in this hall tonight. Everything you crimp after that closes against my counter, and my counter reads your strike underneath it. Any half you set tonight hangs the taped hands with you. You wanted the count off your own mark. It's on it now."

"That's not —" Voss stopped.

"It's how you said it works," Ospina said. "You're the resealing authority. Twice, in Teodoro's drawer."

"I'm a stamp with a grudge in the room," Voss said. "Nothing I crimp is clean."

"Nothing you crimp is alone," Brill said. "That's different, and it's better."

"Kass." Teodoro, fast and pleased with himself, paper moving. "Rings get counted at shift end, but an overflow hand has to sign the overlap to draw one. Shift change on the twenty-first. That's the overlap locker at Anza, and the log that lives in it."

The pump bulb hissed. At the door Saul's pencil came out from behind their ear and stopped.

Kass turned around. "Miko."

Miko had her elbow on the overlap log and her hand flat on the cover, and she looked at Kass's open hand the way a woman prices something she has already paid for twice.

"Rhea," she said. "How many?"

"Three," Rhea said. "Kass, whatever she's about to cost you, cost it."

Voss got up off the bench and went to the end of it, where the crimper stood with its lever up and its cradle empty.

Voss put his hand on the lever. Ospina stepped in front of him, lifted the crescent die from the bench, and seated it in the cradle. The bite in the lower horn caught the light once, then sat dark against the steel.

"Not that one," Voss said.

"That one," Ospina said. "It matches the strike. Pull."

Voss looked at the crescent, then at Ospina's hand on the ring, dull with shop grease and flagged by every desk from here to Kettering. He pulled the lever down.

The crimper closed. The wire bit. The crescent struck its half of the puck while Ospina's live ring closed in the other jaw. Up at the reader bolted to the pump hall wall, the window went amber—steady, not flashing red, not dead. A live counter against a live strike. The ferrule would set. The chain closed.

Brill walked to the chalk line scored into the concrete by the grate. "Saul. Six cases. Scrubbers first."

Saul lifted the tally clipboard. "Which six?"

"The ones by the wall. Corded Anza, pucked Bay 4. Move them before the grade gets a visitor."

Saul's pencil hovered over the log. Then headlights cut through the pump hall's grimy windows—one set, steady, low on the ore grade. Not a ghost train idling at a node. A rig under power, coming up fast.

"Twenty minutes early," Saul said. His pencil stopped.

"Fenn's clearance turns before eight," Kass said, into the set. "That's the desk's clearance. He's not here to watch us load."

Ospina's hand was still on the ring. "He can't stop a crimp already set."

"He can stop the next one," Kass said. "He can take the board. He can take Marlowe. He can write this whole hall off the line."

Rhea's voice came thin through the pump bulb, squeezed between the squeak of the hand pump. "Two restarts. Ivo's down to two. If you're going to finish whatever this is, finish it now."

Ospina didn't move. The amber light held. Voss's hand rested on the lever, halfway down, neither completing the stroke nor releasing it.

"Saul," Brill said. "Load."

Saul took a step toward the stack. The headlights brightened on the grade. One set. Steady. Fenn's clearance was the only thing on this line that turned before eight, which meant when he pulled up to the chalk line, he could write whatever he wanted on it.
